![][image1]**HACKER HANDBOOK**   
**SummerHacks Judging Criteria** 

**Build something fun.** Something that makes you, your friends, or your community smile, laugh, or go  “wait, that’s so cool.” The best projects here come from genuine curiosity and personal spark, so build the  thing you’re actually excited to make, the thing only your team would think to build. 

**Project Submission**

**Track Submission: 11:00PM, August 8th**

[**https://summerhacksca.devpost.com/**](https://summerhacksca.devpost.com/)

Hackers must be registered to the Devpost and formed teams by 11:00PM on August 8th. Teams must submit a project draft containing the tracks they wish to compete in. **Failure to submit will lead to disqualification**

**Soft Deadline: 11:00AM, August 9th**

**Hard Deadline: 1:00PM, August 9th**

Hackers must submit their final project on Devpost by 1:00PM on August 9th. **No late submissions will be accepted after this deadline, including any issues with projects or submissions. This is the final cutoff.**

**The Main Track: What You’re Building** 

**Build a public tool where one moment of human input (a drawing, a photo, a voice clip, a  handwritten word) gets transformed into something that lives online and becomes part of a shared,  growing artifact that anyone can see.** 

Your input can be anything physical. Your transformation can go anywhere. But your output has to be  alive on the internet, contributed to by real people, and feel like it belongs there permanently. Not a demo,  not a prototype, an actual thing people can visit. 

**The Four Constraints** 

**1\. One moment of input.** A drawing. A photo taken right now. A voice clip. A handwritten word held up  to the camera. Contributing should take under 60 seconds and require zero explanation. 

**2\. A non-trivial transformation.** Something interesting has to happen between input and output, and this  is your technical core. It needs to be real, demoed live, and named explicitly on your slide.  

**3\. A stranger sees it.** The result has to be publicly visible: a live website, a shared canvas, a real-time  feed. (Hint: deploy your project…\!) 

**4\. It gets better with more people.** Your artifact should feel richer, stranger, or more meaningful as more  people add to it. Think community garden, not personal diary.  

**Bonus Sponsor Tracks: Stack These With the Main Track** 

You’re automatically eligible for the main track no matter what you build. If your project also fits one (or  both) of the tracks below, you can pick up an *additional* sponsor prize, completely separate from your  main track placement. Nothing here changes what you have to build for the main track. Think of these as  extra ways to get recognized for choices you might already be making. 

 ![][image2]**Best Use of Reve** 

**Rewards visual storytelling and creative transformations.**  
Use Reve to build out your project’s brand and visual identity: illustrations, storytelling visuals, a  distinctive look, so your project doesn’t end up looking like a basic, generic AI-generated frontend. Here,  Reve is a tool you use while building, to raise the craft and personality of what hackers see and interact  with. 

**Where to start:** 

\- Reve’s app: app.reve.com 

\- Getting started guide: help.reve.com, Getting started with Reve 

\- Creating images through chat, custom instructions, aspect ratios, and reference images:  help.reve.com, Creating images on Reve 

**What judges will look for:** 

\- If used as a design backbone: does the project’s visual identity clearly stand apart from a default,  templated AI look?  

![][image3]**TECHNATION: Data Intelligence Track** 

**Rewards projects that collect real usage data and show it back to users visually.** 

If your project naturally generates data about how people are using it, this track rewards you for surfacing  that data in a way people can actually see and explore, not just logging it silently in a database. 

**Where to start:** 

\- **Visualized trends:** where contributors are from, common themes across submissions, usage over  time  

\- **Interactive dashboards:** a live view of what’s happening in your artifact right now  \- **Community sentiment analysis:** surfacing tone, mood, or themes across contributions  \- **Geographic visualization:** a map of where people are contributing from  

\- **Engagement analytics:** contribution counts, growth over the event, peak activity times **What judges will look for:** 

\- The data is real and current, not fabricated or hardcoded for the demo.  

\- The visualization is something users can actually see and explore, not just something you  screenshot for your slides.  

\- The insight is meaningful. It tells people something true and interesting about how the artifact is  being used.  

\- Bonus: the dashboard updates live while judges are watching.  
**The 4 Things Judges Are Scoring** 

![][image4]**Solution Design & Experience, 30%** 

**Did you build something people will love using?** 

Your project should be easy and fun to jump into. A stranger should be able to figure out how to  interact with it in under 60 seconds, with no explanation from you. Make sure your final project  is actually public and live so anyone can try it, not just something you demo from your own  laptop. 

 ![][image5]**Technical Craft, 30%** 

**Did you build it well?** 

Everything you demo should work live. The core transformation of your project, what happens  between someone’s input and the thing that gets created, and something you can explain  confidently. 

![][image6]**Originality & Personal Creativity, 20%** 

**Did you bring your own idea to life, and did it look like it?** 

This category rewards two things equally: your *idea* and how it *looks*. Half your score comes  from having a genuinely original concept, one shaped by your interests, your humor, your friend  group. The other half comes from your visual and creative execution: the design choices, the  aesthetic, the craft that makes your project feel intentional rather than templated. A great idea  with no visual thought behind it, or a beautifully designed but generic idea, will only get you  halfway there. 

![][image7]**Lasting Value & Community, 20%** 

**Would this bring people joy beyond the hackathon?** 

Think about whether your project could become a fun, living thing your community keeps using.  Does it get *better* the more people who use it? Could it realistically keep existing after the  weekend as a fun tool, a shared tradition, a running joke, whatever it becomes for the people who  love it? 

**Before You Get Too Deep In:** 

Every so often, take a step back and ask yourself why you wanted to make this, who it’s for, and  what makes it fun. If your answers still feel personal and genuine, you’re on the right track. The  strongest projects here are the ones that clearly come from something the team actually cares  about. 

One more thing: judges will notice, and mark down, heavy reliance on generic, unedited AI generated visuals. Craft and personal design choices go a long way. Even simple, hand-made  touches beat a default AI aesthetic.  
Now go build something fun. ![][image8]
